name: forwarder-receiver
intent: Hide the interprocess communication mechanism behind two collaborating roles - a Forwarder that marshals a peer's message and sends it to a named remote peer, and a Receiver that unmarshals incoming messages and dispatches them to the local peer - so that application components exchange messages without knowing transports, addresses or encodings.
problem: Components that must talk to each other point to point end up talking sockets: each peer hard-codes the address, the connection handling and the byte layout, so the same component cannot be redeployed over another transport (TCP, Unix domain sockets, shared memory, message middleware) or another platform without editing application logic, and every component duplicates name-to-address lookup, channel establishment and marshalling.
context: Two or more application components exchanging messages in a peer-to-peer fashion, typically in different processes or on different machines, where the IPC mechanism differs per platform or per deployment, where per-message overhead matters (a broker hop or intermediate queue is unwelcome), and where the same peer code should stay usable when the mechanism changes. Common in distributed toolkits, factory-automation and embedded systems, and in agent-style software whose components both request and provide services.
benefits: Transport transparency: peers address each other by logical name and exchange messages; sockets, addressing, connection handling and (de)serialisation live only in the forwarder and the receiver.
Portability and swapping: replacing TCP with Unix domain sockets, shared memory or message middleware changes the two roles, not the peers.
Efficient direct path: a single peer-to-peer hop, with no broker, registry or intermediate queue in the message path.
Marshalling is isolated: one codec pair to fix, version or optimise instead of serialisation code scattered through the application.
Reuse of a proven mechanism: every service in the system gets the same framing, connect and dispatch behaviour.
Testability: peers can be exercised in-process against a fake receiver or forwarder once the mechanism sits behind an interface.
tradeoffs: Every message pays the (de)serialisation cost plus at least one copy; in-process or very high-rate paths are better served by a direct call or shared memory.

The name-to-address mapping is normally static, so adding or moving a peer means a redeployment rather than a lookup; POSA1 states this liability directly as 'no support for flexible re-configuration of components'.

No delivery guarantee at all: a successful send says nothing about arrival (the POSIX send() page notes that 'no indication of failure to deliver is implicit in a send()'), and acknowledgement, retry, ordering and deduplication are absent from the pattern.
Schema coupling: both peers must agree on the message envelope and encoding and version it by hand, so two independently evolving peers break silently.

Unmarshalling is a trust boundary: deserialising attacker-supplied bytes is dangerous (Java's Serializable documentation opens with exactly that warning), so the codec needs validation and allow-listing.
The receiver needs its own thread, event loop or coroutine scope plus a dispatch table, and any state it shares with peer logic needs synchronisation.
Failures look alike at the boundary - a transport error, a codec error and a peer error all surface as 'the message did not arrive' - which is harder to diagnose than a call stack.
Request/reply semantics are not part of the pattern: correlation, timeouts and cancellation must be layered on top of what is fundamentally one-way messaging.

participants.responsibility: Application component that provides or uses services; it sends by calling its forwarder and receives because the receiver invokes one of its methods. It knows nothing about the IPC mechanism.
Resolves the remote peer's logical name to a physical address, marshals the message for the chosen IPC mechanism and sends it; owns the outgoing side of the connection and hides it from the peer.
Waits for incoming messages on the chosen IPC mechanism, unmarshals them and dispatches each one to the peer method responsible for that message.
Maps a peer's logical name to the endpoint the mechanism expects (host and port, socket path, shared-memory segment); static configuration or a lookup service.
Converts peer data structures to and from the wire representation and defines the envelope: message type, framing/length, version and payload.

use_cases: Two processes of one product start on Unix domain sockets on a single host and later move to TCP across hosts; only the forwarder/receiver configuration changes.

Platform-specific IPC: identical peer code runs over shared memory on a real-time target and over sockets in the development environment - the pattern's documented known uses (TASC, the REBOOT material-flow control software, ATM-P) are this class of system.
Agent-style systems in which every component both requests and provides services, e.g. a supervisory cell controller talking to a motion-controller peer.
Replacing a legacy encoding while keeping peers and message contract: swap the marshaller for a portable format (JSON, protobuf, XDR) in the two roles.
A deliberately small first step towards distribution, before a broker, service registry or a full RPC framework is justified.

High-frequency trading or robotics systems where a lock-free SPSC ring buffer in shared memory provides sub-microsecond latency while the forwarder/receiver handles connection establishment and framing.
Game engine multiplayer layers: identical game logic communicates over shared memory on the same host during development and over UDP/TCP for networked multiplayer in production.

Hybrid IPC for high-throughput scenarios: shared memory carries bulk payloads while a Unix domain socket passes the shmid (shared memory segment ID) as a small pointer message to coordinate zero-copy handoffs between processes.
Real-time audio/video processing pipelines where one process decodes and another renders, using shared memory ring buffers for the data path and forwarder/receiver for control messages.
Database client-server protocol implementation where identical SQL client logic runs over shared memory on a single-machine DBMS and over TCP when connecting to a remote server.

Distributed Erlang: processes send to remote pids with the ! operator while net_kernel resolves node names, lazily establishes the TCP connection on first reference and unmarshals on the way in - the ERTS even documents alternative distribution carriers, exactly the transport swap the pattern promises, with the cookie check sitting where the Receiver's validation belongs.

ROS 2 keeps robot nodes transport-agnostic through the rmw middleware interface: client libraries publish, subscribe and call services without knowing the DDS implementation, and the concrete middleware (Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, Zenoh) is swapped by configuration - a production-scale forwarder/receiver role pair per node.

ZeroMQ's brokerless socket topologies (DEP 15/18-style peer-to-peer patterns) apply the pattern's trade directly - application-level request/reply pairs over direct connections with no intermediate queue - and absorb the address book, reconnect and queueing that the raw pattern leaves to the developer inside libzmq.
avoid_when: More than two parties or runtime routing are needed: use a message router, publish-subscribe channel or broker instead of growing the forwarder into a home-made router.
Both components live in one process: a direct call or an in-process queue is simpler and faster.
Peers appear, move and disappear dynamically (elastic scaling, discovery): a registry or lookup service is the missing half of the design.

Messages need persistence, retries, at-least-once/exactly-once delivery or ordering: use messaging middleware (message store, transactional queue, idempotent receiver) rather than rebuilding it inside the roles.
Cross-service schema contracts, streaming and code generation are required: a modern RPC stack supplies the same transparency with far more machinery.
anti_patterns: A forwarder that also decides routing or fan-out to several peers: that is a message router or broker, usually reimplemented badly.
Peers that bypass the roles and open their own sockets 'just for one call', re-coupling the application to the transport.
One Forwarder/Receiver instance shared by several threads or peers without synchronisation, so frames and replies interleave.
Shipping live objects or pointers instead of data (the pass-by-reference temptation of object-RPC systems); the receiver must be able to rebuild the message from bytes alone.
Trusting the wire: unmarshalling untrusted payloads, or rendering a message-supplied type straight into a filesystem path or SQL statement.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: communication mechanics in the roles, application meaning in the peers.
Information hiding and encapsulation: mechanism, addresses and encoding are hidden behind two stable interfaces.
Dependency inversion: peers depend on the message abstraction, not on sockets or a particular communication framework.
Single responsibility per role - the forwarder sends, the receiver listens, the peer decides what a message means.
Stable published message contract: the envelope carries type, framing and version so both sides can evolve independently.
best_practices: Put both roles behind one interface so a second mechanism - and an in-memory fake for tests - can be swapped in without touching peers.
Frame explicitly (length prefix or delimiter); never rely on stream boundaries, and cap the frame size and reject oversized frames.
Version the envelope (message type plus version) and ignore unknown fields so an older peer can still read a newer message.
Validate and allow-list what you decode; never deserialise arbitrary types from the wire, and place TLS/authentication under the roles when the network is not trusted.
Own the receiver's lifecycle: drain, close and join it deterministically, and bound the buffer instead of growing memory on a slow peer.
Decide the disconnected-peer policy up front (fail fast, buffer, retry with backoff) and surface it as a typed error, because the pattern itself provides none.
Keep name-to-address configuration outside the code and version it with the deployment; log the resolved endpoint with every failure.
Use explicit byte-order (big-endian) for all integer envelope fields and validate it at both ends before processing any payload.
Implement keepalive or heartbeat messages on the forwarder/receiver link so that a dead peer is detected within a bounded time rather than waiting indefinitely on a broken socket.
Surface correlation IDs in the envelope so that every logged message carries a traceable identifier linking a peer-side log entry to the forwarder/receiver log entry for the same message.
Handle partial I/O: loop on send and recv until all bytes are transferred or an error occurs; never assume a single call completes a frame.
For high-throughput shared-memory deployments, align hot fields to cache-line boundaries (64 bytes on x86) to avoid false sharing between the forwarder/receiver and the peer.
When combining shared memory with this pattern for bulk data, send only the shared-memory segment ID and offset through the forwarder/receiver channel rather than copying the payload.
sources: Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad & Stal, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns (1996) - Forwarder-Receiver (Design Patterns chapter).

Schmidt, D.C. & Cranor, C.D., 'Half-Sync/Half-Async: An Architectural Pattern for Efficient and Well-Structured Concurrent I/O', PLoPD2 (1996) - related pattern from POSA2 that pairs with Forwarder-Receiver for the Receiver's queueing layer.

Schmidt, D.C., 'Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects' (POSA2, 2000) - covers Acceptor-Connector, Reactor, Proactor, Leader/Followers and Half-Sync/Half-Async which are commonly combined with Forwarder-Receiver.
Douglas C. Schmidt's ACE (ADAPTIVE Communication Environment) framework documentation - implements Forwarder-Receiver pattern in C++ for high-performance network applications.

Anderssén, V., 'Linux IPC Shootout: Shared Memory vs Unix Domain Sockets' (2026) - benchmarks comparing UDS stream/datagram vs shared memory SPSC ring buffer latency and throughput for IPC mechanism selection.
Asadi, B., 'Linux IPC: A Practical Guide to Pipes, Queues, Shared Memory, and Sockets' (2026) - decision matrix and hybrid IPC patterns combining shared memory for bulk data with UDS for signalling.
The Linux Code, 'IPC Through Shared Memory in 2026: Practical Patterns, Pitfalls, and Performance' (2026) - NUMA awareness, robust mutexes, lock-free SPSC ring buffer implementation guidance.

https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/distributed.html - Erlang/OTP 'Distributed Erlang': net_kernel hides TCP/IP behind transparent node-to-node message passing with lazily established connections and pluggable alternative carriers - a production embodiment of the Forwarder-Receiver roles.

https://design.ros2.org/articles/ros_middleware_interface.html - ROS 2 design article on the rmw middleware interface: the vendor-agnostic layer that lets ROS client libraries communicate without knowing the DDS implementation, swappable at deploy time.

http://wiki.zeromq.org/whitepapers:brokerless - ZeroMQ 'Broker vs. Brokerless' whitepaper - the trade-space of brokerless point-to-point messaging: fewer hops and no broker bottleneck at the cost of endpoint-side address management, topology complexity and absent delivery guarantees unless the library adds them.
